pages.body:
Walk past farms in your community and look at the ground. Yam grows on tall heaps of soil, rice stands in flat fields with low walls around them, and tomato seedlings start life on a small shaded bed before they are moved.

- Why do you think farmers do not plant every crop on flat ground?
- What shapes of prepared soil have you seen on farms?

A seed bed is a piece of land that has been prepared by loosening and shaping the soil so that seeds or other planting materials can germinate and grow well. In this lesson we study the types of seed beds, compare them and match each one to the crops and the stage of growth it suits.

We begin with the reasons a farmer prepares the soil before planting.

pages.title: Why seed beds are prepared
pages.body:
- Loose soil lets roots and tubers grow easily.
- Air and water enter loose soil more easily.
- Weeds are removed, so the young crop has less competition.
- The shape of the bed controls water. Raised shapes drain excess water and sunken shapes hold water.
- Manure or compost can be mixed into the soil.

Next we describe each type and say when it is used.

pages.title: Types of seed beds
pages.body:
| **Seed bed** | **Description** | **Best conditions** | **Crops commonly planted** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flat bed | The soil is loosened and levelled at the same height as the ground around it | Well drained soils and areas with moderate rainfall | Maize, groundnut, cowpea, soya bean |
| Raised bed | The soil is heaped about 15 to 30 cm above the ground into a long, flat topped bed with paths between beds | Wet areas, heavy soils and the rainy season, because excess water drains away | Vegetables such as lettuce, carrot, cabbage, onion and tomato |
| Sunken bed | The surface of the bed is lower than the ground around it, with low walls to hold water | Dry areas and the dry season, because water collects and is conserved | Rice, and vegetables under irrigation in dry areas |
| Ridge | The soil is drawn into long, narrow, raised rows with furrows between them | Sloping land and areas where water must be drained or led along furrows | Sweet potato, cassava, maize, tomato, pepper |
| Mound | The soil is gathered into large, round heaps | Shallow or poorly drained soils where deep, loose soil is needed | Yam, cassava, cocoyam, sweet potato |
| Nursery bed | A small, well prepared, shaded bed or seed box with fine soil where seedlings are raised before transplanting | Close to water and protected from sun, heavy rain and pests | Tomato, pepper, garden egg, cabbage, onion, cocoa and oil palm seedlings |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Similarities and differences among seed beds

pages.body:
[[pic: Side view drawings of a flat bed, a raised bed, a sunken bed, a ridge with furrows and a mound, each labelled, with arrows showing how water drains from or collects on each one.]]

Now we compare the seed beds.

pages.title: Similarities and differences among seed beds
pages.body: All seed beds are alike in some ways. In every case the land is cleared, the soil is loosened, weeds are removed and manure can be added. They differ in height, shape, the labour needed and the way they handle water.

| **Feature** | **Flat bed** | **Raised bed** | **Sunken bed** | **Ridge** | **Mound** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Height | Level with the ground | Above the ground | Below the ground | Above the ground | High above the ground |
| Shape | Flat and wide | Long with a flat top | Flat with low walls | Long and narrow | Round heap |
| Drainage | Moderate | Good | Poor, so it holds water | Good | Very good |
| Labour needed | Least | Much | Much | Moderate | Most |
| Depth of loose soil | Shallow | Deep | Moderate | Deep | Deepest |

Finally we match seed beds to the crop and its stage of growth.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Matching seed beds to crops and their stages

pages.title: Matching seed beds to crops and their stages
pages.body:
- Small seeded vegetables are first sown on a nursery bed. At the seedling stage, about three to six weeks later, they are transplanted to raised beds or ridges.
- Root and tuber crops need deep, loose soil for the tubers to swell, so they are planted on mounds or ridges.
- Cereals and legumes with large seeds are sown directly on flat beds or ridges and stay there until harvest.
- Rice needs a lot of water, so it is grown on sunken beds or bunded fields.
- Tree crops such as cocoa, oil palm and citrus are raised in a nursery and later transplanted to the field.
> **Did you know?** Ridges made across a slope, and not up and down it, slow down running water and greatly reduce soil erosion.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Planting Different Crops and Plant Parts on Seed Beds

pages.body:
A farmer plants maize by dropping grains into holes. For cassava she pushes pieces of stem into ridges. For yam she buries a piece of tuber in a mound, and for tomato she first raises small plants and then moves them.

- Why are different parts of plants used to start different crops?
- Which part of the plant is used to grow plantain, sweet potato and pineapple?

Crops are started from different planting materials, and each material suits certain seed beds. In this lesson we study the planting materials, the way each is planted and the seed bed that suits it.

We begin with the parts of plants that farmers use for planting.

pages.title: Planting materials
pages.body:
| **Planting material** | **What it is** | **Crops** | **Suitable seed bed** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Seeds | The part formed after fertilisation, which contains a young plant and stored food | Maize, rice, cowpea, groundnut, okro | Flat bed or ridge, by direct sowing |
| Seedlings | Young plants raised in a nursery | Tomato, pepper, garden egg, cabbage, onion | Raised first on a nursery bed, then transplanted to a raised bed or ridge |
| Stem cuttings | Pieces of mature stem with several buds | Cassava, sugar cane | Ridge, mound or flat bed |
| Vine cuttings | Pieces of a creeping stem with leaves | Sweet potato | Ridge or mound |
| Tubers, setts and minisetts | Whole small tubers or cut pieces of tuber with skin | Yam | Mound or ridge |
| Corms and cormels | Short swollen underground stems | Cocoyam, taro | Mound or flat bed |
| Suckers | Young shoots that grow from the base of the parent plant | Plantain, banana, pineapple | Flat bed, in prepared holes |
| Leaves | A leaf that grows new plantlets | Bryophyllum, also called the miracle leaf | Nursery bed or pot |
| Roots | Swollen roots that sprout new shoots | Sweet potato, breadfruit | Nursery bed, to produce vines or shoots |

Planting with seeds is called sexual propagation. Planting with stems, tubers, corms, suckers, leaves or roots is called vegetative propagation. Plants grown by vegetative propagation are exactly like the parent plant and usually mature faster.

Next we look at how the planting material is put into the seed bed.

pages.title: Ways of planting
pages.body:
- Direct sowing means placing seeds in the field where the crop will grow until harvest. Seeds may be drilled in rows, placed in holes by dibbling or scattered by broadcasting.
- Nursing and transplanting means raising seedlings on a nursery bed and moving them to the field when they have about four to six true leaves.
- Cuttings are planted slanting or upright with about two thirds of the cutting in the soil and the buds pointing upwards.
- Yam setts are placed in the top of a mound, covered with soil and capped with dry grass to keep the soil cool and moist.

Then we list the practices that give the crop a good start.

pages.title: Good planting practices
pages.body:
- Use healthy planting materials that are free from pests and disease.
- Plant at the start of the rains so that the young crop has water.
- Plant at the correct depth. A seed is usually sown at a depth of about two to three times its own width.
- Use the correct spacing so that plants do not compete for light, water and nutrients. Maize, for example, is commonly spaced about 80 cm between rows and 40 cm within a row with two plants on each stand.
- Transplant seedlings in the late afternoon or on a cool, cloudy day, lift them with soil around the roots and water them at once.
- Harden seedlings before transplanting by slowly reducing the shade and the water they receive.
- Replace seeds or plants that fail within the first two weeks. This is called refilling or supplying.

[[pic: Drawings showing maize seeds sown in rows on a flat bed, tomato seedlings being transplanted from a nursery bed to a raised bed, cassava cuttings planted at a slant on ridges and a yam sett placed in a mound with a cap of dry grass.]]

> **Did you know?** In the minisett method, one seed yam is cut into many small pieces of about 25 to 50 grams. Each piece grows into a new seed yam, so a farmer gets many planting materials from a few tubers.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Comparing the Growth of Crops on Different Seed Beds

pages.body:
Two groups of learners plant the same okro seeds on the same day. One group uses a raised bed and the other a flat bed in a low part of the garden that floods after rain. Eight weeks later the plants look very different.

- Which plants do you expect to be taller and to carry more fruits?
- How could the learners show the difference with numbers and not only with words?

A good scientist does not only say that one plant grew better. A scientist measures, records and compares. In this lesson we learn how to measure the growth of crops on different seed beds, present the results in tables and graphs, and explain the differences.

We begin by making sure that the seed bed is the only thing that differs.

pages.title: Setting up a fair test
pages.body:
- Use the same crop and variety, and seeds from the same packet.
- Plant on the same day at the same spacing and depth.
- Give every bed the same amount of water and manure.
- Put the beds in the same part of the garden so that they receive the same sunlight.
- Change only one thing, which is the type of seed bed.

Next we list what to measure and the tool for each.

pages.title: What to measure and how
pages.body:
| **What is measured** | **How it is measured** | **Unit** |
|---|---|---|
| Plant height | Use a ruler or tape from the soil surface to the tip of the main shoot | Centimetres |
| Stem thickness | Wrap a string round the stem just above the soil and measure the string against a ruler | Centimetres |
| Number of leaves | Count the fully opened leaves | Number |
| Leaf size | Measure the length and the greatest width of the largest leaf | Centimetres |
| Number of flowers | Count the open flowers on each plant | Number |
| Number of fruits | Count the fruits on each plant at harvest | Number |
| Yield | Weigh the harvest from each bed on a scale | Kilograms |

Measure at least five plants on each bed every week and work out the average. To find the average, add the values and divide by the number of plants. An average is more reliable than a single plant because one plant may be unusually large or small.

Now we look at a sample set of results and how to present them.

pages.title: Recording and presenting the results
pages.body:
| **Seed bed** | **Average height at week 8** | **Average number of flowers** | **Average number of fruits** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Raised bed | 62 cm | 14 | 11 |
| Ridge | 58 cm | 12 | 10 |
| Flat bed | 45 cm | 9 | 6 |
| Sunken bed | 30 cm | 5 | 3 |

These are sample results for okro grown in a wet season on heavy soil. A bar chart is the best graph for comparing seed beds. Put the seed beds on the horizontal axis and the average height on the vertical axis, and draw one bar for each bed. A line graph of average height against time in weeks shows how fast the plants on each bed grew.

[[pic: Bar chart with seed bed type on the horizontal axis and average plant height in centimetres on the vertical axis, showing bars of 62 for raised bed, 58 for ridge, 45 for flat bed and 30 for sunken bed.]]

Finally we explain why crops grow differently on different seed beds.

pages.title: Reasons for the differences
pages.body:
| **Factor** | **How it affects growth** |
|---|---|
| Drainage | Waterlogged soil has no air, so roots cannot respire and they rot. Raised beds, ridges and mounds drain well in wet weather |
| Water supply | In dry weather raised beds dry out quickly, while sunken beds collect and keep water for the crop |
| Depth of loose soil | Deep, loose soil lets roots spread and tubers swell, so plants take up more water and nutrients |
| Air in the soil | Loose soil holds more air, which roots and useful soil organisms need |
| Soil temperature | Raised soil warms up faster, which speeds up germination and early growth |
| Nutrients | Making ridges and mounds gathers fertile topsoil around the roots |

The best seed bed therefore depends on the crop, the soil and the season. A raised bed that gives the tallest okro in the rainy season may give poor results in the dry season, when a sunken bed keeps more water.

> **Did you know?** Roots need oxygen just as leaves do. This is why most crops turn yellow and die when their roots stand in water for several days.

pages.body:
- A seed bed is land prepared by loosening and shaping the soil so that planting materials can germinate and grow well.
- The main seed beds are the flat bed, raised bed, sunken bed, ridge, mound and nursery bed.
- Raised beds, ridges and mounds drain water and give deep, loose soil. Sunken beds collect and conserve water.
- Vegetables suit nursery beds and raised beds, roots and tubers suit mounds and ridges, cereals and legumes suit flat beds and ridges, and rice suits sunken beds.
- Planting materials include seeds, seedlings, stem and vine cuttings, tubers, corms, suckers, leaves and roots.
- Seeds are sown directly or raised in a nursery and transplanted. Good planting uses healthy materials, correct depth and correct spacing.
- Growth is compared by measuring height, counting leaves, flowers and fruits, finding averages and drawing tables and graphs.
- Differences in growth on different seed beds are caused mainly by drainage, water supply, depth of loose soil, air, temperature and nutrients.
